body.heading: Gratitude with a harvest
paragraphs: North America's Thanksgiving gathers families around the autumn harvest. In Korea, Chuseok does similar work: families travel home, honour ancestors, and share songpyeon — half-moon rice cakes traditionally steamed over pine needles.

The Jewish festival of Sukkot takes meals in a temporary outdoor booth, a reminder of shelter and impermanence. China's Mid-Autumn Festival shares mooncakes under the full moon and gives thanks for reunion as much as for crops.

body.heading: What they all agree on
paragraphs: The details differ — rice cakes, mooncakes, turkey, meals under the stars — but the structure is the same everywhere: pause the year, gather your people, name what the season provided, and eat it together.
It is a template any family can borrow: one meal a year whose real purpose is spoken gratitude. The menu is the easy part.

description: From Sukkot's outdoor booths to Mid-Autumn mooncakes and Korea's Chuseok, harvest gratitude is a worldwide language spoken in food.
